text: In the last lesson you learned two moves: stretching a vector by a number, and adding two vectors tip to tail. That sounds like a modest toolkit, but if you combine the two moves you can reach a surprising amount of space, and the question of exactly how much you can reach turns out to sit underneath every layer of a neural network.

Begin with two special arrows. One points one unit to the right and is called i hat, and the other points one unit up and is called j hat. When we write the vector three, one, what we really mean is: stretch i hat by three, stretch j hat by one, and add the results. The two numbers in the list are instructions for how much of each arrow to use.

Any sum of that kind, some amount of one vector plus some amount of another, is called a linear combination. Think of the two arrows as ingredients and the two numbers as the quantities in a recipe. As you turn the quantities up and down, the tip of the combined arrow wanders around the plane, and with the right recipe it can be made to land on any point you choose.

The set of every point you can reach this way is called the span of the vectors. For i hat and j hat, the span is the whole plane. The same is true for almost any pair of arrows, even crooked ones, as long as they do not point along the same line, because the second arrow always gives you a way to move off the line of the first.

But if the two arrows do lie on the same line, so that one is just a stretched copy of the other, every recipe you mix stays trapped on that line. The second ingredient adds nothing new, and the span collapses from the whole plane to a single line through the origin. When that happens, we say the vectors are linearly dependent: one of them can be built from the other, so it is redundant.

A basis is a set of arrows with no redundancy that still spans the whole space. In the plane, every basis has exactly two vectors, and that count is what we mean by the dimension. Different bases describe the same point with different numbers. The arrow we called three, one becomes two, one when it is measured with a pair of diagonal arrows instead, just as the same distance can be given in kilometres or in miles.

This is exactly how a neural network layer builds its output. Each number the layer computes is a weighted sum of its inputs, a linear combination with learned weights as the recipe. Seen the other way round, the whole output is a combination of a fixed set of arrows, so it can only ever land inside their span. Embedding spaces with hundreds of dimensions give a model a great deal of room, and spanning that room is the same idea you just saw in two.

So a linear combination is a recipe of scaled arrows, the span is everywhere the recipes can reach, and a basis is a smallest set of arrows that reaches everywhere. Next, we let the arrows move. A matrix, it turns out, is nothing more than a record of where i hat and j hat land when space is transformed.
